transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-20
Time: 09:30 PT
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Ellis (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Marco Alvarez (Redwood SE), Sofia Chen (AtlasPay CTO), Liam O'Neil (Platform Eng), Rashid Malik (Security), Grace Park (PM)

Summary section (auto-gen): Quick demo of edge cases around long-context and high throughput. Action items captured.

[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone thanks for joining, I'm Jordan from Redwood Inference, with Priya and Marco from our SE team. Today we'll run through a focused demo on long context, high TPS, streaming backpressure and timeouts. Sofia: thanks, we really want to understand failure modes.

[01:05] Priya: Quick agenda — show Console routing and Optimize suggestions, then API demo for long context, then a load run to illustrate high TPS behavior and how streaming handles backpressure.

[02:12] Sofia: Our use case — payments reconciliation, multi-merchant audit trails, sometimes a single session can hit tens of thousands of tokens, and we also have spikes to 5k TPS across endpoints. Latency target is 200ms p95 for short inferences, but for long context we can accept higher if cost is controlled.

[03:01] Liam: we instrument with envoy and have retries in client, but worried about streaming chunk timeouts and partial outputs causing retries that double load. Also need VPC and KMS details for audit.

[04:18] Priya: got it. Quick note: Redwood supports prefix/KV caching — that reduces repeated prefix cost for long session histories. We also have intelligent batching and per-route autoscale policies.

[05:00] Marco: demoing Console now — routing rules by latency/cost/region, you can pin a route to a quantized variant for cost-sensitivity, and fallback to a higher-capacity model automatically if under-provisioned.

[06:30] Sofia: When you say quantized variant, what's the expected hit on F1/accuracy? We're paranoid about hallucinations for payments text.

[07:05] Priya: typically small delta — we provide model quality profiles based on evals. Also Optimize suggests quant profiles per workload, and we can run regression checks on your prompt set during POC.

[08:22] Jordan: switching to API demo. We'll show streaming response example. Note: streaming is server-sent events over SDKs or web sockets, and we expose chunked tokens.

[09:10] Priya: starting long-context run — we've loaded a 70k token context (simulated multi-merchant log). Notice the KV cache hits for repeated prefixes at ~00:45 in the log.

[10:02] (audio glitch) Speaker 1: ...sorry that was a short drop, go on

[11:15] Marco: As the sequence grows the runtime swaps efficient kernels and does continuous batching. We keep active KV cache across the session so repeated lookups don't re-emit full context. That reduces token work by about 40% in our sample.

[12:40] Sofia: Are there limits on context length? If a single conversation exceeds model window do you chunk or offload to external store?

[13:05] Priya: two approaches — we support sliding window truncation, but for audit workflows we recommend external vector store + summarized context + on-demand retrieval. Also we can surface a 'context overflow' signal so app can decide.

[14:30] Liam: show me how the client handles streaming backpressure — in our current infra the client times out after 15s waiting on a chunk and retries, which causes duplicate work.

[15:12] Marco: demoing a simulated client with small read buffer — when backpressure occurs the server has options: buffer (bounded), apply backpressure via TCP flow, chunk smaller pieces, or close stream with a clear timeout code. Redwood's SDKs emit incremental tokens and include a resume token for retry-friendly partials.

[16:40] Jordan: common pattern we recommend — prefer idempotent/replay-safe requests, use resume tokens for streaming, and on client-side implement exponential backoff with jitter to avoid retry storms.

[18:05] Rashid: For security — does resume token leak PII or session keys? How are tokens encrypted?

[18:45] Priya: resume tokens are opaque server-side references; they don't contain raw payload. All tokens and data at rest can be integrated with customer KMS; plus VPC peering keeps traffic off the public internet. We'll send our KMS integration doc.

[20:00] Sofia: On high TPS — what happens when we push 5k TPS? Do you autoscale instantly or is there a warm window?

[20:40] Marco: Dedicated pools have reserved GPU capacity and configured autoscale (fast scale within minutes). For hosted we do behind-the-scenes capacity juggling and fallbacks — you can set policy to spillover to a cheaper variant or queue. For strict SLOs we recommend Dedicated with pre-warmed burst capacity.

[22:15] Priya: demoing a synthetic load run — we ramp to 5k TPS across three routes and show per-route latency charts. You'll see some tail increases during sudden spikes unless burst capacity pre-warmed. We also show how to configure graceful degradation to return cached responses or smaller models.

[24:45] Sofia: What about client timeouts causing partial responses — is there a recommended timeout value for streaming?

[25:10] Marco: depends on app. For token-by-token streaming we see clients set socket read timeouts of 30s and higher for long contexts. For short ops 2-3s. The SDK exposes heartbeat pings so clients can detect stuck streams earlier and avoid blind retries.

[26:55] Liam: Are there metrics we can surface in our sidecar to avoid unnecessary retries — like 'in-flight token progress' or last-server-seen-offset?

[27:30] Priya: yes, stream progress headers and last-offset are emitted. We can add custom traces into your tracing backend.

[29:00] Jordan: quick security sidebar — SOC 2, audit logs, RBAC, SSO/SAML are supported. For private deployments we do customer-managed control plane and can integrate with HSM/KMS.

[31:20] Rashid: we need to see the audit log format and retention options. We also have to ensure that any on-prem connector doesn't keep transient logs externally.

[32:05] Priya: noted, we'll attach the audit log sample and retention matrix. For POC we can enforce ephemeral logging and stricter retention.

[33:40] Marco: showing Optimize console — it surfaces batching suggestions, quantization recommendations, and per-route unit-cost impact. For your workload we flagged that batch size 8 with prefix caching gives best latency/cost tradeoff.

[35:10] Sofia: ok that helps. Regarding quality, can you run regression tests against our prompt set in the POC? We need to ensure quantized variants don't regress for sensitive outputs.

[36:00] Priya: yes, Optimize can run evals and we can wire your test prompts. We'll include details in the benchmark spreadsheet.

[37:22] (brief crosstalk) Speaker 2: ..sorry micro's a bit low..

[38:10] Jordan: wrapping up demo; capture key failure modes: client retry storms, backpressure & chunk timeouts, large context token cost, and scaling spikes. Recommendations: POC with dedicated test pool, run replayed traffic, use resume tokens and idempotency, configure burst capacity.

[39:45] Liam: one more — what about cost visibility for long-context work? We need token-level attribution per merchant.

[40:12] Marco: Console gives token-level cost breakdown by route and model and you can tag requests with merchant id; Optimize will surface hot merchants driving cost.

[41:50] Sofia: ok actionable next steps?

[42:10] Jordan: we'll send the benchmark spreadsheet, SOC2 + KMS + audit docs, provision POC keys for a dedicated pool for 2 weeks, and schedule kickoff. Priya will be lead SE on the POC.

[43:00] Grace: timeline wise we want to start next Monday if possible.

[43:22] Priya: we can aim for onboarding next Monday — I'll send a runbook and checklist.

[44:05] Rashid: I'll review the security docs and flag any blockers.

[45:30] Jordan: thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the attachments. Any final quick Qs?

[46:10] Sofia: no, looks good, thanks for the thorough demo.

[47:00] Jordan: great thanks, meeting adjourned.
